questions.stem: At year end, Eastmere Partners estimates that $13,700 of its accounts receivable will not be collected. What adjusting entry records this estimate?

options.text: Debit Accounts Receivable $13,700; credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $13,700.
options.misconception: debits the wrong account while leaving the credit unchanged

options.text: Debit Bad Debt Expense $13,700; credit Service Revenue $13,700.
options.misconception: credits the wrong account while leaving the debit unchanged

options.text: Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $13,700; credit Bad Debt Expense $13,700.
options.misconception: reverses the debit and credit sides of the entry

options.text: Debit Bad Debt Expense $13,700; credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $13,700.

questions.explanation: The allowance method records the estimated $13,700 loss by debiting Bad Debt Expense and crediting the contra-asset Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. Directly crediting the receivable would remove a specific account before it is known to be uncollectible, and a revenue credit would misstate the estimate.
questions.hint: The allowance method uses a contra-asset, not a direct write-down.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: A customer balance of $13,000 that had been written off by Goldfinch Co. is later collected in full. Which sequence of entries records the recovery?

options.text: Debit the allowance again at collection without any other step
options.misconception: uses the allowance twice and ignores the cash received

options.text: Credit Bad Debt Expense and never record a receivable
options.misconception: reverses an estimate directly instead of restoring the customer account

options.text: Record only the cash receipt and skip reinstating the receivable
options.misconception: omits the reinstatement step needed to show the original account

options.text: Reinstate the receivable, then record the cash collection

questions.explanation: Recovery requires two steps: first reverse the earlier write-off by debiting Accounts Receivable and crediting the allowance for $13,000, then record collection by debiting Cash and crediting Accounts Receivable. Recording only the cash would lose the history of the restored customer balance.
questions.hint: Restore the receivable before you record the customer's payment.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Goldfinch Manufacturing holds a $12,650 note receivable bearing 6 percent annual interest for 90 days. Using a 360-day year, how much interest will be earned?

options.misconception: uses sixty percent rather than six percent as the rate
uses a full year of interest instead of the 90-day period
inverts the time fraction in the interest formula

questions.explanation: Interest equals principal times annual rate times the fraction of a year, so $12,650 times six percent times 90 over 360 gives $190. Using a full year ignores the short note term, and inverting the fraction would greatly overstate the interest.
questions.hint: Use principal times rate times the fraction of a 360-day year.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: For Holloway Group, the cash account per books is $12,300. The bank collected a $6,450 note for the company and charged a $600 service fee. What is the adjusted book balance?

options.misconception: adds the bank fee instead of deducting it
reverses the additions and subtractions to the book balance
ignores both reconciling items on the book side

questions.explanation: On the book side of a reconciliation, additions such as the $6,450 note collected raise the balance while deductions such as the $600 service fee lower it, giving $18,150. The bank fee is a company expense that must be recorded, not ignored.

questions.stem: Ironwood Enterprises purchased merchandise for $11,950 on terms 1/10, n/30 and paid within the discount period. What amount of cash was paid?

ignores the one percent discount for early payment

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Which control best reduces the risk that an employee of Juniper Works could steal cash receipts and conceal it by failing to record the sale?

options.text: Allowing the cashier to approve write-offs of receivables
options.misconception: gives one person power to hide a shortage through write-offs

options.text: Having the same person receive and deposit cash each day
options.misconception: concentrates duties and increases the opportunity for concealment

options.text: Reconciling the bank account only once every two years
options.misconception: weakens detection by making reconciliation infrequent

options.text: Separating the duties of receiving cash and recording sales

questions.explanation: Segregation of duties makes theft harder to conceal because the person handling cash cannot also alter the records that would reveal a shortage. Combining those roles, reconciling rarely, or granting write-off authority to a cashier all concentrate power in ways that weaken internal control.
questions.hint: No single person should both handle an asset and record it.
